```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

Many questions about human-AI interaction are comparative: whether learners
who received AI feedback regulate their work differently from those who did
not, whether a tutoring dialogue changes as learners gain experience, or
whether the division of labor between a programmer and a coding assistant
shifts over a course. In a heterogeneous transition network each of these
questions becomes a comparison of two weight matrices that share the same
codes and the same actor partition. The comparison has three parts, which
answer different questions and should not be confused. A descriptive
comparison says how similar the two networks are and where their
differences lie. A permutation test says whether the differences are larger
than the variation expected between two random halves of the same sessions.
A Bayesian comparison says how large each difference plausibly is and how
precisely the data estimate it.

This guide applies the three comparisons to the early and late sessions of
the bundled vibe-coding data. In a heterogeneous network the descriptive
comparison has one further element that a homogeneous network lacks: the
differences can be summarized by actor-pair block, separating changes in
how each actor continues its own work from changes in how the actors hand
over to each other.

```{r package}
library(htna)
```

## Data

`human_ai` holds 429 sessions of human-AI pair programming, coded into six
human and six AI codes. Each row is one coded event.

- **Session**: `session_id`; the unit that is resampled and permuted.
- **Code**: `code`; the node of the network.
- **Actor type**: `actor_type`, `"Human"` or `"AI"`; the actor partition.
- **Order**: `order_in_session`; the position of the event in its session.
- **Cohort**: `phase`, a factor with levels `Early` (the first 214 sessions
  in chronological order) and `Late` (the remaining 215).

One network is built per cohort with `group`. The cohorts follow the levels
of `phase`, so every comparison below is `Early` minus `Late`.

```{r build}
data(human_ai)
grp <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type", group = "phase")
```

## How similar are the two networks?

`compare_htna()` computes the descriptive comparison of every pair of
cohorts in a grouped network; here there is one pair. Printing the result
gives the correlation and mean absolute difference of the edge weights and
the summary of the differences in each actor-pair block.

```{r compare}
cmp <- compare_htna(grp)
cmp
```

The two networks are close: the Pearson correlation of their 144 edge
weights is 0.959 and the mean absolute difference is 0.0192, on a scale on
which every row of transition probabilities sums to one. The actor-pair
table locates the differences. Because each row sums to one, the within-actor
and between-actor blocks of the same source actor are mirror images: the
mean difference is 0.00622 per cell in the AI-to-AI block and -0.00622 in
the AI-to-human block. Summed over the six target codes, an AI code was
followed by another AI code with a probability about 0.037 higher in the
early sessions than in the late ones (6 x 0.00622), and handed back to the
human correspondingly less often. The changes for human source codes are
smaller (0.00168 per cell). The largest single difference, 0.181, lies in
the AI-to-AI block.

The full set of similarity, correlation and distance measures is returned
by `as.data.frame()` with `what = "metrics"`.

```{r metrics}
as.data.frame(cmp, what = "metrics")
```

The rank-based measures agree with the Pearson correlation (Spearman
0.9365, cosine similarity 0.9744), and the rank agreement of the edges is
0.8788. The descriptive comparison therefore shows two
networks with the same overall structure and modest differences
concentrated in what the AI does after its own moves.

The edge-level differences behind the block summaries are in the edge
table, one row per edge, with both weights and the actors of the edge.

```{r edges}
head(as.data.frame(cmp, what = "edges"))
```

A scatter plot of the edge weights of the two networks shows the same
agreement graphically: points on the diagonal are edges with equal weights.

```{r scatter, fig.height = 5}
plot(cmp, type = "scatter")
```

## Are the differences larger than chance?

A descriptive difference can arise from sampling alone. `permutation_htna()`
pools the sessions of both cohorts, reassigns them at random to two groups
of the original sizes, and rebuilds both networks 500 times. Each edge's
observed difference is compared with the differences between the shuffled
networks, and the networks as a whole are tested with the sum (M) and the
maximum (S) of the absolute differences. Because whole sessions are
shuffled, the nesting of transitions in sessions is respected.

```{r permutation}
perm <- permutation_htna(grp, iter = 500, seed = 1)
perm
```

The global test rejects the hypothesis that the two cohorts come from the
same process: the summed absolute difference M = 2.760 has p = 0.002 and the
largest difference S = 0.181 has p = 0.016. At the level of single edges, 30
of the 135 tested edges have an unadjusted p-value below 0.05.
`plot_htna_diff()` draws these edges with the actor layout of the network:
green edges are stronger in the early sessions, red edges in the late ones.

```{r permutation-plot}
plot_htna_diff(perm)
```

With 135 tests, about seven edges would fall below 0.05 by chance alone, so
the individual edges have to be read with a correction for multiple
testing. The Benjamini-Hochberg correction controls the false discovery
rate.

```{r permutation-bh}
permutation_htna(grp, iter = 500, seed = 1, adjust = "BH")
```

After the correction no single edge remains significant, while the global
test is unchanged. The cohorts differ as wholes, but the evidence is spread
over many small edge differences rather than concentrated in a few strong
ones. Statements about individual transitions changing between the phases
are not supported by this test; the statement that the interaction changed
is.

## How large are the differences, and how precisely are they estimated?

The permutation test answers whether a difference exceeds chance, not how
large it plausibly is. `bayes_compare_htna()` models the transitions out of
each code as a multinomial draw with a Dirichlet prior and gives, for each
edge, the posterior mean difference, a 95% credible interval and the
probability that the difference lies on its side of zero.

```{r bayes}
bc <- bayes_compare_htna(grp, draws = 4000, seed = 1)
head(summary(bc))
```

The first rows show the information the permutation test lacks. The
transition from `Ask` to `Execute` is 0.0214 more probable in the early
sessions, with a credible interval from 0.00897 to 0.03355 that excludes
zero, while the larger difference for `Ask` to `Plan` (0.0477) has a wider
interval, from 0.0067 to 0.0868. The number of edges flagged as credibly
different is counted with `xtabs()` on the summary table.

```{r bayes-count}
xtabs(~ sig, data = summary(bc))
```

Thirty-four edges have credible intervals that exclude zero and pass the
default thresholds. No correction for multiple comparisons is applied, and
the model treats every transition as an independent draw, ignoring the
nesting of transitions in sessions; the count is therefore larger than a
corrected permutation test would give and should be read as a ranking of
where the differences are largest. The two analyses largely agree on which
edges these are:

```{r agreement}
both <- merge(summary(perm), summary(bc), by = c("from", "to"))
xtabs(~ sig.x + sig.y, data = both)
```

Of the 30 edges with an unadjusted permutation p-value below 0.05
(`sig.x`), 28 are also credibly different in the Bayesian comparison
(`sig.y`). The grouped Bayesian result is drawn in the same way as the
permutation result.

```{r bayes-plot}
plot_htna_diff(bc)
```

## Which comparison to use

| Question | Function | Reads |
|---|---|---|
| How similar are the networks, and in which actor-pair block do they differ? | `compare_htna()` | `print()`, `summary()`, `as.data.frame(x, what = )` |
| Do the networks differ more than chance, overall and edge by edge? | `permutation_htna()` | `print()` (global test), `summary()`, `plot_htna_diff()` |
| How large is each difference, with what uncertainty? | `bayes_compare_htna()` | `summary()`, `plot_htna_diff()` |
| Which longer patterns differ between the cohorts? | `sequence_compare_htna()` | see [Sequences and patterns](sequences-and-patterns.html) |

The three comparisons are complementary and are best reported together:
the descriptive comparison for the size and location of the differences,
the permutation test with a multiple-testing correction for the inferential
claim, and the Bayesian intervals for the precision of individual edges.
When the cohorts contain repeated sessions of the same people, pass
`actor` to `permutation_htna()` so that whole persons are shuffled.
Comparisons of more than two cohorts work in the same way and return one
result per pair; the [Case study: early and late sessions of vibe
coding](case-early-late.html) interprets this comparison in substantive
terms.
